title: Turn a Good Intention into an If-Then Plan
subtitle: Pre-decide one safe response to one clear cue.
description: Turn a repeated low-stakes choice into a simple cue-and-action rule, add a fallback for common exceptions, and revise the rule when it creates friction or no longer fits the work.

lifeOsSource.hack: For a recurring low-stakes decision, write one clear cue and one pre-decided action so you do not have to invent the response from scratch each time.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one repeated situation, describe the cue in observable terms, choose a small action you can safely perform when the cue appears, add a fallback for a common exception, use the rule when the situation occurs, and revise or retire it when it stops fitting the work.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did the cue occur, did I follow the chosen action, what exception appeared, and should the rule stay, change, or be removed?
lifeOsSource.reference: Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer (2024) — Meta-analysis of implementation intentions across 642 independent tests

faq.question: What makes a useful cue?
faq.answer: Use something you can recognize without interpretation, such as a meeting ending, a task entering a particular status, a file arriving, or a deadline reaching a defined checkpoint.

faq.question: Should the rule always be followed automatically?
faq.answer: No. The rule is a convenience for a recurring low-stakes choice. It should never override safety, access controls, approvals, contractual duties, or new information that materially changes the situation.

intro.html: An if-then rule is useful when the same small decision keeps returning. Instead of re-deciding from zero, you define the cue and a reasonable response in advance. The rule stays subordinate to context: it should be easy to revise, easy to stop, and narrow enough that exceptions are visible.

sections.title: 1. Choose one recurring situation
sections.html: Pick a moment that appears often enough to be annoying but is still low stakes: a meeting ending, a request waiting for clarification, a task becoming blocked, or a routine handoff. Avoid building a rule around rare or consequential decisions that deserve fresh judgment.

sections.title: 2. Write the cue and the action
sections.html: Make the cue observable and the response concrete. For example: If a meeting ends with an unresolved owner, then I add an owner question to the follow-up before closing my notes. The action should be small enough to execute without creating a second planning problem.

sections.title: 3. Add one important fallback
sections.html: Name a common condition that should suspend or redirect the rule. A fallback might be an approval requirement, unavailable information, an urgent interruption, or a handoff to another owner. The fallback prevents a convenient shortcut from becoming blind automation.

sections.title: 4. Keep only rules that still fit
sections.html: When the cue occurs, use the rule and notice the result. If the rule repeatedly creates cleanup, gets ignored, or no longer matches the workflow, narrow it, replace it, or remove it. A deleted bad rule is an improvement.

references.title: The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests
references.claim_scope: Meta-analysis of 642 independent tests supports implementation intentions as a self-regulation strategy and finds stronger average effects for contingent if-then formats. Aggregate results do not guarantee success for every goal, population, cue, or productivity task.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported effect-size claims, fabricated outcomes and observations, health-adjacent triggers, wearable thresholds, and rigid repetition schedules with a bounded cue-action decision rule for ordinary work.
